newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African govt spending, slow reform under fire.
newsitem.headline: S.African govt spending, slow reform under fire.

text.p: South Africa's Board of Executors (BOE) on Tuesday warned the long-term consequences of the government's failure to curb spending and its slow pace of economic reform could mean more interest rate rises this year.
In its latest investment outlook, BOE added that the rand would remain "extremely vulnerable" this year.
Despite certain positive short-term signs, BOE said it remained "deeply concerned about the longer-term outlook for economic performance and the currency."
Short-term financial stabilisation depended entirely on "a substantial slowdown in domestic economic growth, and domestic spending, in particular.
"We believe there is a significant risk that this slowdown in spending may not occur with sufficient rapidity," it said.
The Reserve Bank's September quarterly bulletin indicated that private sector wage increases per worker rose to 12.3 percent in the first quarter.
"Even with the inflation rate rising towards the eight-percent level, this still represents a substantial real increase," BOE said.
Government spending also began rising again in real terms and by the second quarter was 2.1-percent higher than a year ago, adjusted for inflation.
"Total government spending in July and August was up 22 percent on the same months a year ago," it said, attributing the gain mostly to wage and salary rises and higher developmental spending.
But "private consumption spending is being slowed by high interest rates and high debt levels, but this is being partly counterbalanced by rising public sector expenditure," BOE said.

"The next few months will reveal whether the current levels of interest rates and the currency are sufficient to maintain financial stability and in turn, generate the conditions for lower interest rates in the future.
"There is a risk that they are not."
Reserve Bank figures also showed employment falling. The strong rise in the number of public sector jobs in the 12 months to March 1996 was more than offset by private sector job losses.
But BOE said "The already unstable socio-political situation can do no other than deteriorate in conditions of continuously rising unemployment.
"It is a pipe dream to assume sustained foreign capital inflows in future years in this case.

"We therefore continue to urge policymakers to implement a much more aggressive economic reform programme than currently envisaged to dramatically raise the sustainable economic growth rate," it said.
Despite this, policy makers continued to insist privatisation would be gradual and the relaxation of exchange controls would be delayed by pressure on the currency.
An increase in VAT had also been ruled out, even in the March 1997 budget, despite BOE estimates that a two-percent increase was "essential to give credibility to fiscal policy."
Foreign exchange reserves remained low and would be "precarious" for the foreseeable future, BOE said.

In the "unlikely" event foreign inflows exceeded current account deficits, these would be needed to allow the Reserve Bank to withdraw from the forward cover market and prepare for the next step in the removal of exchange controls.

"In the absence of a meaningful economic reform/stabilisation package, it is possible that interest rates may yet have to be increased, while the scope for reduced interest rates is both limited and at best some months away," BOE said.
